archetype.name: Fringe Contender (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose top-three passing offense wins shootouts and keeps it in the playoff race, while a bottom-three defense keeps its true efficiency closer to average than its 4-2 record suggests.

report.headline: Top-three offense, bottom-three defense: a 4-2 record built on shootouts.
report.take:
Detroit is back to the shape of its 2022 team, when the offense ranked 6th in EPA and the defense 31st. The offense is elite again. It ranks 3rd in EPA per play, 2nd in passing EPA (0.309) and 2nd in success rate, and it scores 30.7 points a game. Jared Goff has started every game and thrown for 1,788 yards. The targets run through Amon-Ra St. Brown, with Jahmyr Gibbs, Sam LaPorta and Jameson Williams behind him, and Gibbs carries the ground game almost alone. The defense is the problem. It ranks 30th in EPA allowed and 28th against the pass, gives up 27.5 points a game, and opponents throw on it more than almost anyone in neutral situations. Every game except the Green Bay win went over the total.

The record is mostly honest. Wins over expected sit at just 0.22, and the point differential implies 3.8 wins against the actual four. The efficiency underneath is thinner, though. Net EPA is -0.002, 19th, which is the profile of a .500 team. The gap between that and a +19 differential comes from things that are real but fragile: special teams ranked 2nd, a +0.5 turnover margin a game, and an offense that has turned the ball over only three times. The market has noticed. Detroit has been favored in five of six games and covers at a 0.2 rate, 30th in the league, because it keeps winning by less than expected or losing outright, as it did at Carolina.

Two defensive numbers flatter the unit. Detroit leads the league with 21 sacks and misses the fewest tackles, yet its pressure rate is only 18th. Sacks are piling up faster than the pressure behind them, and that usually cools off. The coverage is what actually breaks down. Deep passing EPA allowed is 28th, TE1s are scoring 7.9 PPR points over their average (31st), and third downs (28th) and red-zone trips (27th) are converting freely. Kerby Joseph has not played yet, so some of this could be personnel. Still, the 2025 defense was only 15th and this one is worse.

The Green Bay game is the warning sign for the offense. Goff threw for 303 yards, but the run game posted -15.5 EPA and there were two turnovers. That came in Detroit's first game after losing guard Ben Bartch, a 93%-snap starter, to IR. The line's run blocking was already odd: it ranks 4th in yards before contact but 28th in stuff rate and 30th in short yardage. That weakness matters most against defenses that win at the line, and the next one is the best in football.

strengths.title: Goff's passing game is top-two
strengths.body: Detroit's dropbacks are among the league's most productive. It ranks 2nd in passing EPA and 2nd in overall success rate, and it has played balanced rather than leaning on pass volume. Clean pockets drive it: the line allows the 5th-lowest pressure rate. Its 2024 offense ranked 3rd by the same measure, so this isn't new and should hold.

strengths.title: Sacks and sure tackling
strengths.body: The defense leads the league in sacks and in fewest missed tackles. It finishes the plays it gets to, and it doesn't let short throws turn into long ones after the catch. The tackling is a sustainable skill. The sack total is less so, because the pressure rate behind it is only 18th. Expect fewer sacks per game from here.

strengths.title: Special teams tilting the field
strengths.body: Special teams add 4.64 EPA a game, 2nd in the league. That is a big part of why the point differential runs ahead of a neutral net EPA. It's a real edge, but special-teams value swings from week to week and is a shaky thing to count on.

concerns.title: A pass defense that bleeds big plays
concerns.body: Opponents pass on Detroit more than almost any team in neutral situations, and they're right to. Pass EPA allowed is 28th, deep EPA allowed 28th and explosive pass rate 28th. Tight ends and secondary receivers are getting loose: WR2 EPA allowed ranks last and TE1 EPA allowed 31st. Kerby Joseph's eventual return could help. Until then, the shootouts will keep coming.

concerns.title: Can't get off the field
concerns.body: Opponents convert 47.7% of third downs (28th) and score touchdowns on 72% of red-zone trips (27th). Those failures in high-leverage spots turn decent defensive stretches into 30-point allowances. With only six takeaways (24th), the defense isn't erasing drives any other way.

concerns.title: Short-yardage run game, now without Bartch
concerns.body: Gibbs gets help before contact, but the run game gets stuffed too often and converts short yardage at the 30th-best rate. Losing Bartch, a 93%-snap guard, until late November coincided with a -15.5 rushing EPA game against Green Bay. One game isn't a trend. It is a soft spot heading into a stretch of strong fronts.

trend.note: The defense has improved over the last two games, allowing 21 and then 17 after giving up 30-plus three times. The offense moved the other way, scoring 45 at Arizona and then only 20 against Green Bay, when the run game collapsed.

nextGame.headline: Goff's passing game against the league's best pass rush decides it
nextGame.body:
This is strength on strength and weakness on weakness. Minnesota is 6-0 behind the NFL's best defense: 1st in EPA allowed against both pass and run, 1st in pressure rate, 1st in red-zone TD rate, and 12.3 points allowed a game. Its offense ranks 29th in EPA and dead last in success rate. The perfect record leans on luck the Vikings won't keep getting: 2.52 wins over expected (1st), a perfect record in one-score games and a league-best turnover margin. Detroit is the better team by the Book's view (DET -3, 46.5 total) mainly because its offense is so far ahead of Minnesota's. The Lions' bad pass defense is facing an offense that struggles to sustain drives.

Availability favors neither side cleanly. Detroit is without guard Ben Bartch (IR) heading into a matchup with the league's best pressure unit. St. Brown is questionable with an ankle he tweaked against Green Bay, but Campbell expects him to practice Thursday. Kerby Joseph remains out, and corner Ennis Rakestraw is questionable after leaving the Packers game, though the injury isn't believed to be major. Minnesota has lost guard Donovan Jackson to IR. Aaron Jones is questionable but day-to-day. Kyler Murray has started every game since Week 2.

waysToWin.title: Win through the air, not the ground
waysToWin.body: Opponents run against Minnesota more than against any other defense, and it hasn't worked: rush EPA allowed ranks 1st. The coverage has a crack at the top, though. WR1s produce 0.43 EPA per target against Minnesota, 24th in the league. With a healthy St. Brown and an offense 2nd in passing EPA, Detroit should lean pass-heavy early.

waysToWin.title: Sack Murray and stall drives
waysToWin.body: Minnesota's line allows a sack on 9% of dropbacks, 30th in the league. Detroit's 7.2% sack rate means its rush finishes when it gets home. Against an offense that ranks last in success rate, a couple of drive-killing sacks could be enough to keep the score in the low 20s.

waysToWin.title: Protect the ball, force Minnesota to score
waysToWin.body: Minnesota's offense scores just 20.8 points a game and has needed short fields and takeaways to win. Detroit has committed only three turnovers all season. A clean game would make the Vikings drive the length of the field, which they rarely manage.

waysToLose.title: Pressure and takeaways swamp Goff
waysToLose.body: Minnesota pressures on 34% of dropbacks and hits the QB more than anyone, and it has 11 takeaways. Detroit's protection is 5th in pressure allowed, but it is now missing a starting guard. Two turnovers against Green Bay showed what happens when drives get knocked off schedule.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone trips end in field goals
waysToLose.body: Minnesota allows touchdowns on just 23.1% of red-zone trips. Detroit's short-yardage run game is one of the league's worst, and its stuff rate is 28th. If drives stall inside the 20, Detroit's yardage won't turn into a margin Minnesota can't overcome.

waysToLose.title: Bad offense, big plays, long drives
waysToLose.body: Detroit's deep coverage ranks 28th and its third-down defense 28th, with Joseph still out and Rakestraw banged up. Minnesota ranks 3rd in time of possession. A few chunk throws and third-down conversions would let a weak offense control the clock and keep Goff off the field.

nextGame.watch: Detroit's interior pass protection without Bartch against Minnesota's league-best pressure rate, especially on third down.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable part. Elite passing efficiency behind a clean pocket was Detroit's identity in 2024 too. The schedule also offers soft spots in Miami, Tennessee and Tampa Bay, though Tampa's defense ranks 3rd, along with a home date with New England. The defense is likely to stay below average, but it should get a little less bad. Its sack pace should cool toward what an 18th-ranked pressure rate supports, while its takeaway count (24th) has room to rise, and Joseph's eventual return helps the secondary.

The back half is heavy with divisional road games: Minnesota, Chicago and Green Bay all away in the final four weeks. A net-EPA-neutral team can't count on special teams and turnover margin to keep covering its defensive leaks. Expect more shootouts and a record that settles in the playoff-bubble range, not a return to 2024.
swingFactors: Bartch's return and the line's short-yardage play
Whether the secondary stabilizes once Joseph returns
Turnover margin and special teams holding up

confidence.note: Six games, a consistent QB and a familiar offensive profile, but the defense and special teams numbers are still noisy.
